projectDesc.p: Encoded for the Experiencing War web site for the Veterans History Project.

samplingDecl.p: The recording of the interview with Robert Cox was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: Donna Trotman
sp.p: Good afternoon. Today is May 28th, 2010. My name is Donna Trotman. I am conducting an oral history interview at the Court Reporting Institute of Dallas in Dallas, Texas, with Robert Cox. Please state your name and address for the record.

sp.speaker: Robert Cox
sp.p: It's Robert M. Cox. 3618 Crestview Drive, Garland, Texas, 75042.

sp.speaker: Donna Trotman
sp.p: Awesome. You still live in Texas. That's great. Okay. So, I'm gonna ask you a few questions. Were you drafted, or did you enlist?

sp.speaker: Robert Cox
sp.p: I enlisted.

sp.speaker: Donna Trotman
sp.p: You enlisted. Where were you living at the time?

sp.speaker: Robert Cox
sp.p: At Hot Springs, Arkansas.

sp.speaker: Donna Trotman
sp.p: And why did you join?

sp.speaker: Robert Cox
sp.p: It's like all young guys; I wanted to get that war over with and punish a bunch that -- that needed punishing.

sp.speaker: Donna Trotman
sp.p: Very nice. And why did you pick the service branch?

sp.speaker: Robert Cox
sp.p: Well, I just turned 17, so they said you was gonna have to go into the Navy. In other words, if you were gonna wait until the Army, you'd have to wait till you get 18 where you could drafted or something. So, I selected the Navy.

sp.speaker: Donna Trotman
sp.p: Nice. Do you recall your first days in service?

sp.speaker: Robert Cox
sp.p: I sure do.

sp.speaker: Donna Trotman
sp.p: What did it feel like?

sp.speaker: Robert Cox
sp.p: Well, I -- they put me on a train from Little Rock, Arkansas, and on my way to San Diego. But we lived like a king, because the Navy bunch had separate apartments, where the poor Army and the rest of them had many people sleeping in these cars. And pulled into San Diego, and, of course, they referred to you as a "boot". So, that's what I was for a few weeks there when I was taking the training. So I'll never forget that.

sp.speaker: Donna Trotman
sp.p: Do you remember any of your instructors?

sp.speaker: Robert Cox
sp.p: Not by name, but most of them were Chief Petty Officers, that had our classes and the whole works, really. That took us under hand and tried and teach us everything we didn't know.

sp.speaker: Donna Trotman
sp.p: And how did you get through your boot camp and/or training experience?

sp.speaker: Robert Cox
sp.p: Oh, I got -- good. Of course. I was a -- like a wise kid there for a while, but they took that out of me real fast. So it didn't take me long to shape up.

sp.speaker: Donna Trotman
sp.p: Which war did you serve in?

sp.speaker: Robert Cox
sp.p: Well, I was in World War II, Korea, and Vietnam.

sp.speaker: Donna Trotman
sp.p: Wow. That is a lot, goodness. Do you remember arriving in each of those places?

sp.speaker: Robert Cox
sp.p: Oh, yes. Yes. Yes. Because when I arrived in the Navy, when I finished my schooling, I went to -- and, of course, I'll always remember it because it was a lepper colony. A French lepper colony. And of course I waited there to be assigned to the ship, the USS _. So, I will never for get that.

sp.speaker: Donna Trotman
sp.p: What was your main job?

sp.speaker: Robert Cox
sp.p: My main job, when I went aboard, was what they called the Black Gang. I was in the fire room. That's where all your machinery, as far as running your generators, everything for your guns, and the steam for the power of the ship. So it was the heart of -- between the fire room and engine room, it was responsibility of seeing everything was maintained on board the ship.

sp.speaker: Donna Trotman
sp.p: Wow. During that time did you get to see combat?

sp.speaker: Robert Cox
sp.p: Yeah. We had 13 battle scars.

sp.speaker: Donna Trotman
sp.p: Were there any casualties in your unit?

sp.speaker: Robert Cox
sp.p: Oh, we were fortunate. Yes, we had some -- our first person was killed, was the Japanese Betty flew over and machine gunned him. That was our first one. And, of course, I say God flew with our bunch because the ship I was on, which was the command ship of the four cruisers, and the rest of those ships got pretty well -- lot of people killed. But God, I think, was with us and kept us safe. _ Of course, we were hit with torpedos, which -- duds. Which, I say the man was looking after us, but, of course we -- one of your job -- my job when I first went aboard the cruiser was casualties to -- someone got shot we had to go -- you know -- top side to take care of him. So, I learned it had hard way -- 17 year old. But say, that was _ my experience.

sp.speaker: Donna Trotman
sp.p: So you were 17 when you first saw your --

sp.speaker: Robert Cox
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Donna Trotman
sp.p: Do you have any more memorable experiences that you don't think you'll ever forget?

sp.speaker: Robert Cox
sp.p: Well, I'll tell you the first one. As I said, when they was -- told us that there was torpedos -- 2 torpedos coming to us, of course, I just kind of laughed. One of the officers grabbed me and throw me down on the deck. And _ you hear: "Thunk. Thunk", and that was it. That was it. As I said, someone was looking after us. And, of course, as I say, we had the Kamikazes hit around our ship and, of course, we were fortunate there. We, of course, got hit, but nothing to sink us. So that was a memory I'll always remember more than anything. And, of course, the other thing I remember was we had the -- take the -- I was also on barrel detail, which we went down below and they sewed them up in the canvas and put a 5 inch _ at their feet. And one thing I'll never forget -- Of course, in that day, like everything else, I tried to smoke a little bit. I had a Zippo lighter, and I reached over to pick up the body, and my lighter fell down where he was, and it stayed -- it went down in the sea with him because I wasn't about to reach in get it. But I'll never for get that.

sp.speaker: Donna Trotman
sp.p: Whenever those - those torpedos didn't go off -- they were the duds -- was --what war was that?

sp.speaker: Robert Cox
sp.p: That was in World War II. And the Air Force most -- well it was up in Alaska, and I was in recon outfit, and we were picked up a by couple of medics, Russian medics. And we were fortunate we had one old boy on there was a CFC gunner, was a World War II boy, and the rest of them kind of froze, but he didn't freeze. He cut that B50 _ .50 caliber machine guns at the medics. Of course, _ we went as steep a dive as you could get to get out of the there. So, I'll never forget that. As I said, the man was with us.

sp.speaker: Donna Trotman
sp.p: Were you ever a prisoner of war?

sp.speaker: Robert Cox
sp.p: No. Thank God.

sp.speaker: Donna Trotman
sp.p: That's right. Were you awarded any medals?

sp.speaker: Robert Cox
sp.p: Well, we got quite a few medals. Like I said, I couldn't _ bring them here today because we did know -- of course, as I said, that many years in the service, you're gonna accumulate some medals. But I guess my Unit Citation from World War II is most memorable. You know, I honor it more than any of them.

sp.speaker: Donna Trotman
sp.p: Did you have -- did you have close touch with your family?

sp.speaker: Robert Cox
sp.p: The only thing I had back then was, of course, letters. And, of course, the mail didn't come very often, but, when it did, you looked forward to it.

sp.speaker: Donna Trotman
sp.p: What was the food like?

sp.speaker: Robert Cox
sp.p: Well, if you ever read this war diary, you can see it wasn't the most pleasant deal, because when you was in battle, of course, the only thing you would get was a sandwich, and they give you maybe a cookie or apple or something, and that's what you survived on. You would get pretty hungry.

sp.speaker: Donna Trotman
sp.p: So you didn't eat three times a day?

sp.speaker: Robert Cox
sp.p: Not all the time.

sp.speaker: Donna Trotman
sp.p: What book is that?

sp.speaker: Robert Cox
sp.p: This here was written by one of the boys aboard the ship. He keep record -- he kept records. He's dead now. Which was -- really it's against taboo to do it during war time, you know -- you know, write something down you did every day, but he did. Of course, he got permission after the war was over to print it, and out of the process -- proceedings he got for this thing, he didn't keep it for himself, he gave it to charity. And that is -- I still enjoy reading it, because it's from our battle -- It started from _ Canal on up, and, of course, he did. He'd set there and sneak, and everybody always wondered what he was doing. But that's what he was doing, he was writing notes for prosperity after the war, which we enjoyed it now.

sp.speaker: Donna Trotman
sp.p: So you were friends with him?

sp.speaker: Robert Cox
sp.p: Well, the ship had a lot of people on it. They were in different divisions, but you got to knowing them, but you can't say, “Well, hey. This is my buddy” or something, because he was just the friend that you knew of. Of course, I was below deck all the time. Temperatures around 130 at all times. Of course, the gunners, and stuff, they were all topside. And, of course, all the time I was aboard ship was over 3 years, but they never slept below deck. It was too hot, but you go up topside and tried to find you a place to sleep which was half-way cool and the Pacific wasn't that cool.

sp.speaker: Robert Cox
sp.p: Do you feel you had plenty of supplies in the wars.

sp.speaker: Donna Trotman
sp.p: Oh, yes. Yes. Yes. Yes. When we needed ammo -- Of course, we'd run short once in a while and, of course, we'd get a _ ship come along side, and everybody had to -- you know, to standby and help load, and you can see me carrying a 130-something pound projector, and I weighed 132 pounds. It was pretty rough, I'll tell you.

sp.speaker: Donna Trotman
sp.p: Did you feel the pressure or stress of situation around you?

sp.speaker: Robert Cox
sp.p: No I don't. I don't. I've -- I guess I've been cold natured every since the war, I mean, don't forget, I've got feelings, but stuff don't bother me.

sp.speaker: Donna Trotman
sp.p: How did you deal with that?

sp.speaker: Robert Cox
sp.p: Well, I just -- everyday day. It just -- something that I guess I got my body acclimated to between the Navy and Air Force that's just normal routine for me.

sp.speaker: Donna Trotman
sp.p: Was there something special you did for good luck?

sp.speaker: Robert Cox
sp.p: Well, I guess I did. Of course, I was a protestant but the captain we had aboard the ship was a Catholic. And when the first battle was into I said, "Padre, what's your religion?" He said, "I'm Catholic." And I said, "I am too." Which, I wasn't naturally, but I took him -- make me feel like I was safe with him. I'll be frank with you.

sp.speaker: Donna Trotman
sp.p: On your ship, how did people entertain themselves?

sp.speaker: Robert Cox
sp.p: Well, we was fortunate, once in a while, when we'd get back from battle zone, they'd have a movie on topside, and that was, of course, the only entertainment you had. You didn't -- you just kept busy, because we still didn't know what to call -- four on and eight off, that was continuously.

sp.speaker: Donna Trotman
sp.p: What does that mean?

sp.speaker: Robert Cox
sp.p: That means the first watch was on, you was on 4:00 to 8:00, and 8:00 to 12:00, and 12:00 to 4:00. That just ever -- That's _ routine. One week you was on the 4:00 to 8:00, and the next time was 8:00 to 12:00, the next one was 12:00 to 4:00. Just a routine that you just got into, and that's the way you stayed. You kept busy enough that you didn't get to -- have time to, you know, worry about anything.

sp.speaker: Donna Trotman
sp.p: Gosh. What did you do when you went on leave?

sp.speaker: Robert Cox
sp.p: Well, all I got to come home -- leave one time. The ship had been hit, and we came back to _ Island for repairs, and I got to go on leave, which I enjoyed very much. _ go back to Hot Springs and, of course, weren't there for long, then back then to California.

sp.speaker: Donna Trotman
sp.p: Where did you travel while you were in the service?

sp.speaker: Robert Cox
sp.p: Well, I traveled all the through the South Pacific, and, of course, when I was in the Air Force, I seen England, Japan, Alaska; operating out of there, and and South America.

sp.speaker: Donna Trotman
sp.p: A lot of places. Do you recall any particularly humorous or different odd event happening?

sp.speaker: Robert Cox
sp.p: Well I guess it was, I used to enjoy, once in a while, they'd have a US hope tour come on the islands, and get to go over on -- see some of the old movie stars, long before you your time, but we enjoyed them.

sp.speaker: Donna Trotman
sp.p: Did you have movie stars like come and --

sp.speaker: Robert Cox
sp.p: Oh yeah. Joey -- names your not gonna familiar. Joey Brown and, he's a comedian, and, of course, a lot girls come out. Of course, we wouldn't _ Well now, in the air force we had Bob Hope. So, we enjoyed that quite a bit I'm sure.

sp.speaker: Donna Trotman
sp.p: Do you have photographs?

sp.speaker: Robert Cox
sp.p: Oh yes. I have some of the photographs. Of course, I got my book. That was about the _. Which its got -- got all of our ship mates and pictures and stuff was taken in the battles and whatnot. That -- Baker Division. I don't know if that's up there or not. At the bottom of the page that's the outfit I was in. Yeah, Baker.

sp.speaker: Donna Trotman
sp.p: So these are all the people --

sp.speaker: Robert Cox
sp.p: Yeah. This is me here. A lot them boys, of course, are dead now.

sp.speaker: Donna Trotman
sp.p: Look at you.

sp.speaker: Robert Cox
sp.p: Well, hun, that was a hundred years ago.

sp.speaker: Donna Trotman
sp.p: What did you think of officers or fellow soldiers?

sp.speaker: Robert Cox
sp.p: Oh, yeah. Well, we all got along good especially in the Navy. We had some -- we had fine officers, and, of course, the Air Force we had great officers. _ flight engineer for on the B-50s and what not, B-29s. So, we all had a good work agreement with everybody and enjoyed one another.

sp.speaker: Donna Trotman
sp.p: So did you guys work together?

sp.speaker: Robert Cox
sp.p: Oh, you had to work together, especially on flight crew, because you depend on one another to do a job to stay going, because, like I said, I was flight engineer, which I had to control the engine and whatnot, and, of course, it all depended on me, and I depended on them to make sure I got home safe.

sp.speaker: Donna Trotman
sp.p: I know your friend, or the other soldier, kept a diary. Did you personally keep a diary?

sp.speaker: Robert Cox
sp.p: No. No.

sp.speaker: Donna Trotman
sp.p: Okay. So, we're gonna talk a little bit about after your service. Do you recall the day your service ended

sp.speaker: Robert Cox
sp.p: Oh, yes. Yes. I retired one day and went to work for _ TV the next day. I stayed with them for 24 years.

sp.speaker: Donna Trotman
sp.p: So, where were you when you ended?

sp.speaker: Robert Cox
sp.p: I retired when I was in the Wichita Falls. I was in sack for 18 years. That's in the -- of course, the Air Force. In the Navy, of course, after the war was over we got discharged, and I was out a while, and I come on back in and reenlisted.

sp.speaker: Donna Trotman
sp.p: So you reenlisted?

sp.speaker: Robert Cox
sp.p: Into the Air Force. See if I stayed in the Navy, I'd be the type aboard ship all my life and I couldn't see that. That ain't no place for a person. You know, for getting married and have a family.

sp.speaker: Donna Trotman
sp.p: What did you do in the days and weeks afterwards. After you started at the other company?

sp.speaker: Robert Cox
sp.p: Well, as I say, I was on -- The Air Force. I retired from the Air Force. I didn't get that much time because, like I say, I quit -- retired one day, and went to work for _ the next day which was aerospace.

sp.speaker: Donna Trotman
sp.p: Did you go back to school?

sp.speaker: Robert Cox
sp.p: I took a lot of courses.

sp.speaker: Donna Trotman
sp.p: Was your education supported by the GI Bill?

sp.speaker: Robert Cox
sp.p: Well, no. No, because, as I said, I -- most of them I took when I was in service which they took care of it, in other words, there wasn't no GI Bill type. And the short time I was out, I didn't utilize the GI Bill for, you know, classes, because I got my diploma with a GED. Because, as I say, when I went in, I was -- didn't quite finish high school, because I wasn't, oh, but, what, you know, 17, and I didn't quite make it. So, when I come back, of course, I was a little -- naturally, a few years older, and I really got out Navy. But I didn't wanna -- right at that particular time, you know go to school. But, then I seen I needed the education. So, I -- I got back in the Air Force, I went -- You know, it was studies to get a GED. And, plus, as I say, I took a lot -- all different kinds of courses that were required in the service. I went to a lot of service schools. Which, as I say, went to Flight Engineers, which was a 9 month school, where I was a Panel Op -- What they call a Panel Operator which was the B59s and B50s. And then we go into the Jet Age, it was a little different and, of course, I got into a higher bracket, as far as jobs, different jobs. And maintenance and whatnot.

sp.speaker: Donna Trotman
sp.p: So its what we would kind of call on the job training?

sp.speaker: Robert Cox
sp.p: Oh, most everything you do in the service is on the job training.

sp.speaker: Donna Trotman
sp.p: Did you make any close friend ships while were in the service?

sp.speaker: Robert Cox
sp.p: Oh, yes. Yes. Yes. Yes. I still -- A bunch of us still get together. Especially the Navy, because I loved them guys because they were my age. We was all say 17 years old. And we kind of stuck together, and we still stick together. Of course, as I say their dying off every day, but the one's that's left, we still get together.

sp.speaker: Donna Trotman
sp.p: That's amazing. Did you join a veteran's organization?

sp.speaker: Robert Cox
sp.p: Oh, yes. I belong to VFW and American Legion. Pretty active in it.

sp.speaker: Donna Trotman
sp.p: Does that mean that you go and support other troops that are --

sp.speaker: Robert Cox
sp.p: Well, we support troops and go out to the VA Hospital and have Bingo for them, and just anything we can, you know, to help the troops. You know, we still are veterans.

sp.speaker: Donna Trotman
sp.p: And you're understanding of what they go through.

sp.speaker: Robert Cox
sp.p: That's right, especially these kids now days when they can't just shoot one another. Someone's gotta blow them up.

sp.speaker: Donna Trotman
sp.p: Did your military experience influence your thinking about war or about the military in general?

sp.speaker: Robert Cox
sp.p: Well the other thing is I believe in, of course, a strong military which is taught me to defend our country and to take care of people that tries to do something to our country. So I feel strong about that.

sp.speaker: Donna Trotman
sp.p: Do you attend reunions?

sp.speaker: Robert Cox
sp.p: Reunions? I sure do. This is the last one for the Navy, because, oh, there's not many of us left that was aboard the ship, the _. And I used to go to the Air Force reunions, but I spent most of my time with the Navy because, as I said, those are the ones I felt so close to all my life.

sp.speaker: Donna Trotman
sp.p: How often --

sp.speaker: Robert Cox
sp.p: Every -- A reunion every year. And that's been going on for a long time but you can say, _ age. A lot of them's are older than I am and you figure, of course, I'm old. And, it just ain't enough of us to keep it going any more. And, of course, the young kids, our kids, our grand kids, of course, they don't have the deal where they like to, you know, continue it. So, as I said, this is our last year for the Navy Reunion.

sp.speaker: Donna Trotman
sp.p: I'm sorry to hear that.

sp.speaker: Robert Cox
sp.p: I am too.

sp.speaker: Donna Trotman
sp.p: How did your service and experiences affect your life?

sp.speaker: Robert Cox
sp.p: Well, I think it taught me a lot. It -- more for -- Of course, I'm such a strong believer of our country. And, of course, it's taught me to, as far as the kids we send, see if we can get everything they need for their duty. So, that's where it's taught me a lot.

sp.speaker: Donna Trotman
sp.p: Did you feel that way before --

sp.speaker: Robert Cox
sp.p: It made me a better man, too.

sp.speaker: Donna Trotman
sp.p: Did you feel that way beforehand -- about how you felt about our country?

sp.speaker: Robert Cox
sp.p: Oh, I always felt, as a kid I felt -- I pretty much was taught about God and country. So, this just made it stronger to me, I think, all these years.

sp.speaker: Donna Trotman
sp.p: Is there anything you would like to add that we have not covered in this interview?

sp.speaker: Robert Cox
sp.p: No. I think you've covered about everything, dear.

sp.speaker: Donna Trotman
sp.p: Thank you so much for coming. I really appreciate it.

sp.speaker: Robert Cox
sp.p: Well, I appreciate you -- y'all asking us over.

sp.speaker: Donna Trotman
sp.p: It was an experience. Thank you so much, Mr. Cox. A. Thank you, dear.
